596.title: The mind unshaken
596.hook: the last blessing: a mind the world's ups and downs can touch but not shake
596.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the eight worldly conditions as a daily reflection, and the Mangala Sutta's closing verses are chanted in full at blessings across Theravada countries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the blessings of the heart, and your line, gratitude is a blessing. Did you tell someone exactly what they did for you? Today, the blessings poem reaches its last verses. Day five hundred ninety-six.

Monday: a compliment from the boss. Tuesday: a client complains. Wednesday: a bonus. Thursday: a bill twice what you expected. Friday: your post goes semi-viral. Saturday: someone you like unfollows you. Sunday: a headache. One week, and the mood has ridden up and down like a cheap elevator. Nobody gets to choose which floor the day stops on. The Mangala Sutta, after company and learning and home and heart, ends with a blessing about exactly that elevator. Today: the mind unshaken.
screen: `MONDAY UP, TUESDAY DOWN.` → `A CHEAP ELEVATOR.` → `THE POEM'S LAST BLESSING.`

segments.voice: The poem climbs to its peak in two verses. First: discipline, a pure life, seeing the noble truths, and realizing nirvana. That is the highest blessing. Then the verse this lesson is named for. Whose mind, when touched by the ways of the world, does not shake. Free of sorrow, free of stain, secure. That is the highest blessing. The ways of the world have a name in Buddhist teaching: lokadhamma, the worldly conditions. There are eight, in four pairs. Gain and loss. Fame and obscurity. Praise and blame. Pleasure and pain. Elsewhere the Buddha says these eight come to the untaught person and to the wise disciple alike. Nobody gets only the good half. Look at the exact words. The mind is touched. The verse doesn't say the world stops reaching you, or that you stop feeling. Praise still arrives; so does blame. The difference is that the mind doesn't shake. Like a well-rooted tree in wind: the leaves move, the trunk stays. And then the poem's last verse gathers everything up. Those who have done these things are undefeated everywhere, and go everywhere in safety. Theirs is the highest blessing. That's the poem's arc in four days: from the company you keep, to your home, to your heart, to a mind steady enough to stand in any weather. Not luck. Not omens. A life built so well that the elevator can go up and down, and you can stay standing inside it.
screen: `SEEING THE TRUTHS, REALIZING NIRVANA` · `EIGHT WINDS: GAIN, LOSS, PRAISE, BLAME` · `TOUCHED, BUT NOT SHAKEN` · `UNDEFEATED, SAFE EVERYWHERE` · then, large: `UNSHAKEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay steady, starting with the breath. Sit and settle. Recall one recent up, a compliment, a win. Feel how it lifts you. Breathe, and let it be touched, not grabbed. Now recall one recent down, a criticism, a loss. Feel how it pulls. Breathe, and let it touch too, without shoving it away. Up and down, the winds blow. Feel the part of you that stays where it is: the breath, the seat, the steady trunk. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Lokadhamma, the worldly conditions. The last blessing of the Mangala Sutta: touched by gain and loss, praise and blame, pleasure and pain, and still not shaken. Today's word.
Your line: unshaken. When today's elevator jolts, up or down, name the wind under your breath, praise, blame, gain, loss, and feel your feet. Day five hundred ninety-six.

fork.reveal: the verse says the mind is touched by the worldly conditions but does not shake: sorrowless, stainless, secure.

597.title: The old way
597.hook: elderly brahmins ask whether their people still live the way the ancient sages did
597.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics live on alms and own very little, and lay Buddhists often take extra precepts on observance days to practice simplicity, such as eating before noon and setting aside entertainment and adornment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last blessing, and your line, unshaken. Did you name a wind and feel your feet? Today, some old men ask a brave question about their own tradition. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

Lots of families keep a founder story. Great-grandparents who arrived with one suitcase and worked six days a week and never wasted bread. Companies have them too: two people in a garage. So do schools and congregations. And sooner or later someone asks the uncomfortable question: are we still like that? A group of elderly brahmins from Kosala, wealthy and well respected, come to the Buddha with exactly that question about their own people. Do the brahmins of today live by the ways of the brahmins of old? It takes courage to ask. Today: the old way.
screen: `A FOUNDER STORY.` → `ARE WE STILL LIKE THAT?` → `ELDERS FROM KOSALA ASK.`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers gently, and mostly with praise for the past. The sages of old, he says, were self-controlled and austere. They had no cattle, no gold, no stored grain. Learning was their wealth, and they guarded it like treasure. Food was set out for them at doors, given with trust. Nobody turned them away. They spent their youth in study and pure living. When they made offerings, they offered rice, bedding, clothes, butter and oil, and no cow was killed. Cows, the poem says, were like mothers and fathers and brothers to them, friends who gave food, strength, beauty and ease. Then the poem tells a story of change. In time, those sages saw the splendor of kings: fine clothes, chariots, beautiful houses. Desire for that life crept in. Sacrifices grew grand and costly, and animals began to be killed at them. And the poem says that when the knife fell on the cow, the gods themselves cried out that it was wrong. The elders who asked the question are moved, and they take refuge. Notice how the Buddha answers. The poem is sharp about the drift, but he doesn't scold the men in front of him. He answers their question with their own ancestors, and holds up a picture any tradition, any family, any of us might recognize: a simple beginning, slowly filled with comfort and display, and elders brave enough to ask. In this poem, simplicity and self-control aren't a new teaching. They're the old one.
screen: `NO CATTLE, NO GOLD: LEARNING WAS WEALTH` · `OFFERINGS WITH NO ANIMAL KILLED` · `THE SPLENDOR OF KINGS, AND DRIFT` · `ELDERS BRAVE ENOUGH TO ASK` · then, large: `THE OLD WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice simply. Sit and settle. Think back to when you first started something that mattered: a friendship, a job, a faith, a hobby. What was it like at the beginning, before it filled up with extras? Notice one simple thing you've drifted from. Maybe it's just doing the thing, without the gear, the audience, the upgrades. Breathe with that beginning for a moment. Then choose one way to do it the old, simple way today. The bell holds the time.
Porana, the ancient ones. The Buddha's picture, for elders who asked, of the simple, self-controlled life of the ancient sages, and of how easily anyone drifts from it. Today's word.
Your line: plainly, without extras. Do one thing today the way you did it at the start, just for itself. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

what a scholar hears: the Brahmanadhammika Sutta (Sn 2.7) praises the brahmins of old and places the drift with King Okkaka's great sacrifices, where the gods cry out at the killing of cows.

598.title: The boat
598.hook: a swimmer swept away in a flood can't save anyone; a skilled boatman can carry many
598.howItsDone: Buddhists often describe the teaching as a way of crossing to the far shore, and many communities stress studying with a qualified teacher before teaching others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the elders' brave question, and your line, plainly, without extras. Did you do one thing plainly, as at the start? Today, a river in flood, and two people trying to cross. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

Every lifeguard learns it early: a drowning person will pull a rescuer under. You don't jump in after someone unless you know what you're doing, because two people in trouble don't make one rescue. In the Ganges plain, in the rainy season, rivers rose fast and wide, and crossing was a real danger. Everyone knew the difference between a person thrashing in the current and a ferryman standing in a sturdy boat. The eighth poem of the second chapter builds a whole teaching on that difference. Today: the boat.
screen: `A LIFEGUARD'S FIRST RULE.` → `RIVERS RISING IN THE RAINS.` → `THE THRASHER AND THE FERRYMAN.`

segments.voice: The poem starts with teachers. Honor the person you learn the truth from, it says, the way the gods honor their king. A teacher who is honored, and pleased, opens up what they know. A student who listens closely becomes wise and skilled too. Then the warning. If you follow someone who hasn't understood, a small-minded person who hasn't really grasped it, you'll end up the same: still full of doubt. And then the picture. Someone falls into a river in flood, the current fast and wide. They're swept along, helpless. How could they carry anyone else across? Then the other picture. Someone climbs into a strong boat, with oar and rudder. They know the river. They know the method. That person can carry many others across. The same, the poem says, with someone who truly knows, who has trained and listened deeply and isn't shaken. They can help others understand, if others are willing to listen. Notice the order of the poem. First you need a good teacher. Then you need to actually learn. Only then can you carry anyone. It's a gentle warning against rushing to help before you're steady yourself, and it's also a promise: once you are steady, your skill isn't only for you. The boat holds more than one. In daily life it can look small. A friend who came through a divorce sits with another friend going through one. A nurse on her tenth night shift talks a new nurse through his first. Each of them knows this stretch of river.
screen: `HONOR THE ONE YOU LEARN FROM` · `A FOLLOWER OF THE CONFUSED STAYS CONFUSED` · `SWEPT AWAY, OR IN A STRONG BOAT` · `STEADY FIRST, THEN CARRY OTHERS` · then, large: `TAKE OTHERS ACROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone across, starting with your own boat. Sit and settle. First, steady yourself. Feel your feet, your seat, the breath going in and out: oar and rudder. Then think of something you've genuinely learned to cross: a hard season, a skill, a fear. Now think of someone still in that river. What's one small thing you know that would help them? A tip, a phone call, a calm word. Choose it. The bell holds the time.
The boat. The poem's picture of someone who has truly learned: steady in a strong boat, with oar and rudder, able to carry many across the flood. Today's word.
Your line: take others across. Offer your one helpful thing today to the person still in that river. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

599.title: The poet's question
599.hook: the monk-poet Vangisa asks what became of his teacher who has died
599.howItsDone: Buddhists remember teachers who have died with memorial offerings, chanting and merit dedications, and many monasteries keep the death anniversaries of their teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the boatman, and your line, take others across. Did you offer your one helpful thing? Today, a grieving student, and a question asked in verse. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

When someone who taught you dies, a strange question can rise up, one you might not say out loud. Where are they now? Did they get where they were going? Were they at peace? Among the Buddha's monks was a man named Vangisa, who'd been a wandering poet before he ordained. Words came to him fast, in verse, and the Buddha praised him for it. Vangisa's own teacher, an elder named Nigrodhakappa, has just died. Vangisa sits alone, and the question comes. He doesn't keep it to himself. Today: the poet's question.
screen: `WHERE ARE THEY NOW?` → `VANGISA, THE MONK-POET.` → `HIS TEACHER HAS DIED.`

segments.voice: Vangisa goes to the Buddha and asks, as a poet would, in verse. He starts with praise, the way you'd open a letter to someone you love. You who cut through doubts, he says, a monk has died here, known and honored, peaceful. Then he asks the real thing. Was my teacher fully freed? Or did something still bind him? Did he cross over, or is there more to his journey? And he says what's at stake: all of us here want to hear it. It's a brave question, the kind that can go unasked for fear of the answer. Vangisa asks it, and asks beautifully. The Buddha's answer is short. He cut off craving for this world of name and form, the stream that had run in him for a long time. He crossed over birth and death completely. And Vangisa's joy comes pouring out in more verses. My question wasn't wasted, he says. I wasn't let down. Notice two things. First, the poem lets trust and an open question sit in the same person. Vangisa trusts the teaching, and he still needs to ask. Second, his love for his teacher comes out as art. He doesn't just wonder; he writes. At a funeral, words can run out. Vangisa's didn't, and he gave them to his teacher. This poem is a student honoring his teacher, and asking out loud what everyone around him wanted to know.
screen: `A POET'S PRAISE, LIKE A LETTER` · `WAS MY TEACHER FULLY FREED?` · `HE CROSSED BIRTH AND DEATH` · `TRUST AND A QUESTION, TOGETHER` · then, large: `THE POET'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line for a teacher, starting now in your head. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone who taught you something that lasted: a parent, a coach, a teacher, a grandparent, living or gone. See their face clearly. What did they give you? Let one sentence form, no need for it to be perfect. Just one true line, the way Vangisa would. Say it silently to them. Later today, you might write it down. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Vangisa. The monk-poet, grieving his teacher, asking the Buddha in verse whether he was freed, and turning his love into words. Today's word.
Your line: my question wasn't wasted. Write your one line for that teacher today, on paper or in a message, and if they're living, consider sending it. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

600.title: The promise kept
600.hook: the oldest telling of the young wanderer and King Bimbisara, and what happened years later
600.howItsDone: Buddhists remember King Bimbisara's gift of the Bamboo Grove to the community, and pilgrims to Rajgir in India visit both the Bamboo Grove and the hills where the young wanderer is said to have met the king.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vangisa grieving his teacher, and your line, my question wasn't wasted. Did you write your line? Today, day six hundred, a new chapter, and a scene you first met long ago. Day six hundred.

Way back, on day forty-one, a young wanderer walked through Rajagaha with his bowl, and a king on a palace terrace couldn't stop watching him. The king offered him an army and a fortune. The young man said no. That was more than a year and a half ago on this path. Today we open the Great Chapter of the Sutta Nipata, and its first poem is that same scene, in what may be one of the oldest tellings of it we have. We'll hear it in its own plain words, and then we'll follow the story forward, to what happened when the wanderer came back. Today: the promise kept.
screen: `DAY 41: A KING ON A TERRACE.` → `THE GREAT CHAPTER OPENS.` → `THE STORY, FORWARD.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Pabbajja Sutta, the going forth. Tradition says Ananda speaks it. King Bimbisara sees a young man walking for alms, eyes lowered, looking only a plow's length ahead. He sends messengers, who find him eating on a hillside outside the city. The king drives out, steps down from his chariot, and makes the offer: you're young, noble-looking, lead my army, take wealth. The young man answers simply. My people live beside the Himalaya, he says, among the Kosalans, rich and energetic, Sakyans by birth. I didn't leave home to find pleasures. I've seen the danger in them, and the safety in letting go. I'm going to strive. That's where my heart is glad. And the poem ends there. Notice what it doesn't include. In this old poem, there's no promise to return. That comes in later tellings: the king asks him, if you find what you seek, come back and teach me first, and he agrees. And the monastic texts tell how it was kept. After awakening, the Buddha walked back to Rajagaha. The king came out to hear him with a great crowd, and understood. Then Bimbisara said that as a young prince he'd had five wishes: to be crowned, that an awakened one would come to his kingdom, that he could honor him, that he'd be taught, and that he'd understand. All five, he said, have come true today. He gave the community a park, the Bamboo Grove, and the Buddha accepted it. A promise made on a hillside, kept years later.
screen: `EYES LOWERED, A PLOW'S LENGTH AHEAD` · `I DIDN'T LEAVE HOME FOR PLEASURES` · `THE PROMISE COMES IN LATER TELLINGS` · `FIVE WISHES, ALL COME TRUE` · then, large: `THE PROMISE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall day forty-one, and your own promises. Sit and settle. Picture the hillside: a young man with a bowl, a king stepping down from his chariot. Two people who would meet again. Now think of a promise someone kept to you, maybe years later than you expected. If gratitude comes, let it. Then think of one promise you've made and haven't yet kept, small or large. Don't scold yourself. Just hold it gently, and see the first step back toward it. The bell holds the time.
Pabbajja, going forth. The young wanderer refuses a king's fortune, and in later tellings promises to return; awakened, he comes back, and all five of the king's wishes come true. Today's word.
Your line: take the first step. Toward the promise you're still holding today: a call, a date set, a start. Day six hundred.

601.title: Mara's generals
601.hook: in one of the oldest tellings, Mara's army has no elephants: it's desire, discontent, hunger, craving, sloth, fear and doubt
601.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the list of Mara's armies to help meditators recognize hindrances as they arise, and Mara's defeat is a common subject of temple murals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the king's five wishes, and your line, take the first step. Did you take one step toward yours? Today, the wanderer is alone by a river, and someone comes to talk him out of it. Day six hundred one.

Some voices that stop you aren't angry at all. They're kind. You're worn out, one says. Look at you. Take a break. You've done enough. Why push so hard when you could be doing something nice and useful instead? On day fifty-two we met Mara, the tempter, and his later, enormous army of elephants and storms. Today we hear what may be one of the oldest poems about Mara and the wanderer, the Padhana Sutta, the discourse on striving. And here, Mara opens with sympathy. Today: Mara's generals.
screen: `THE KIND VOICE: TAKE A BREAK.` → `DAY 52: ELEPHANTS AND STORMS.` → `AN OLDER TELLING.`

segments.voice: By the Neranjara river, the wanderer is striving hard, thin from fasting. Mara, here called Namuci, comes with gentle words. You're thin and pale. Death is close. Live, sir! Living, you could do good deeds and earn merit. Why struggle? The answer is firm. I don't need merit, he says. I have faith, I have energy, I have wisdom. As my body wastes, my mind grows clearer. And then he names the army, one rank at a time. Desire is your first army. The second is discontent. The third, hunger and thirst. The fourth, craving. The fifth, sloth and drowsiness. The sixth, fear. The seventh, doubt. The eighth, contempt and stubbornness. And then: gain, fame, honor, a reputation wrongly won, praising yourself and looking down on others. This, Namuci, is your army. Notice who the generals are. Not demons from outside. Every one of them can turn up inside an ordinary person, on a slow afternoon. Discontent. Drowsiness. Fear. Doubt. Even fame and praise are in the ranks. Then the line the poem turns on. On the old Indian battlefield, the commentary says, a soldier who would never retreat tied a tuft of munja grass to himself as a sign. Should I wear the munja grass? Shame on a life lived defeated. Better for me to die in battle than to live beaten. And the poem's end: Mara says he followed the Buddha for seven years and never found an opening. He's like a crow pecking at a stone that looked like fat. He drops his lute and disappears.
screen: `THE KIND VOICE: LIVE, WHY STRUGGLE?` · `DESIRE, DISCONTENT, HUNGER, CRAVING` · `SLOTH, FEAR, DOUBT, CONTEMPT, FAME` · `THE MUNJA GRASS: NO RETREAT` · then, large: `BETTER TO FIGHT THAN YIELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one of Mara's generals. Sit and settle. In the next two minutes, one may well show up. Discontent: this is boring. Drowsiness. Doubt: what's the point? A craving for your phone. When one arrives, don't fight it with force. Just name it, quietly, by rank: ah, the fifth army, or there's doubt. Naming takes away its disguise. Then come back to the breath, and stay. That staying is the munja grass. The bell holds the time.
Mara's generals. In the Padhana Sutta: desire, discontent, hunger, craving, sloth, fear, doubt, contempt and the pull of fame, an army that lives inside. Today's word.
Your line: better to fight than yield. When the kind, tired voice says give up on something good today, name the general, and stay one minute longer. Day six hundred one.

602.title: Well spoken
602.hook: speech that is well spoken, pleasant, true and in line with the teaching
602.howItsDone: Right speech is the third factor of the noble eightfold path, and many Buddhists, lay and ordained, keep a precept against false speech; teachers often give the four marks of well-spoken words as a test before speaking.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mara's generals, the army with names like craving, sloth, fear and doubt, and your line, better to fight than yield. Which general showed up for you? Today closes a week, and it's about the mouth. Day six hundred two.

Please pass the salt. Running late. Sounds good. A day's talk is mostly words that vanish the moment they're said. A few stay. A sentence someone said to you as a kid can still be sitting there decades later, for good or for ill. Speech is something people do all day, often without thinking, and the early Buddhist texts give it close attention. In the third chapter of the Sutta Nipata there's a short discourse that sets out what makes speech good. It has four marks, and a poet stands up at the end. Today: well spoken.
screen: `WORDS THAT VANISH.` → `A FEW STAY FOR YEARS.` → `SUTTA NIPATA 3.3.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells the monks that speech with four marks is well spoken, blameless and not faulted by the wise. The monk says only what is well spoken, not what is badly spoken. Only what is in line with the teaching, not what goes against it. Only what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant. Only what is true, not what is false. Four filters, and every sentence has to pass all four. Then something lovely happens. Vangisa, the poet monk you met three days ago asking after his teacher, stands up and says: something has come to me. And he puts the teaching into verse on the spot. Speak only words, he says, that don't torment yourself and don't harm others. Speak pleasant words, words people are glad to hear, without bringing in anything bad. Truth, he says, is the deathless word; on truth the good stand firm. Notice what this is not. It isn't flattery: pleasant is joined to true. And it isn't blunt honesty with no care for the listener: true is joined to pleasant. The two hold each other in check. Look back at the week. A mind unshaken. The old way of the brahmins. The boatman who takes others across. Vangisa's question about his teacher. The young wanderer's promise to a king, kept. And Mara's generals. Today the poet comes back, still finding the right words.
screen: `FOUR MARKS OF GOOD SPEECH.` · `WELL SAID, THE TEACHING, PLEASANT, TRUE.` · `VANGISA PUTS IT IN VERSE.` · `TRUTH IS THE DEATHLESS WORD.` · then, large: `WELL SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak well once. Sit and settle. Bring to mind one conversation you'll have today, at work, at home, on the phone. Pick one thing you'll need to say in it. Now run it through Vangisa's test, gently. Is it true? Will it harm the person hearing it, or you? Can it be said in a way they'd be glad to hear, without bending the truth? Find the words, then let them go and rest with the breath. When the moment comes, they may be ready. The bell holds the time.
Well spoken. In the Sutta Nipata, speech that is well said, in line with the teaching, pleasant and true, all four at once. Today's word.
Your line: true and kind. Today, say one thing that is both, on purpose, to someone who will be glad to hear it. Day six hundred two.

fork.setup: you're Vangisa. the Buddha has just finished teaching four marks of good speech, and a verse is rising in you. what do you do?
options: keep quiet; it isn't your place.
stand, say something has come to you, and speak it in verse.
write it down later for yourself.
fork.reveal: he stands, tells the Buddha a verse has come to him, and is invited to speak it. the teaching gets its poem on the spot.

original.note: Pali subhasita: well spoken. the Subhasita Sutta is Sn 3.3.

trapdoor: what you thought: good speech just means not lying.
what it means: four marks at once: well said, in line with the teaching, pleasant and true, each keeping the others in check.
what a scholar hears: the Subhasita Sutta (Sn 3.3) is also found in the Samyutta Nikaya, in the section of verses connected with Vangisa (SN 8.5).
